Utilizing $B^0_s\gamma\gamma$ decay data from the CMS experiment at the LEP, a study was conducted to determine the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay length, resulting in an estimate of $\Gamma(B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$) as 0.313±0.004 (model-based)±0.026 (statistical)±0.009 (systematic) meV.

This research focuses on a discrete version of a dissertation problem related to the optimization of a performance indicator for a system managed by local controllers in a distributed way. The system being controlled exhibits stochastic behavior and is modeled using a Markovian framework. Initially, the optimal control strategy for the continuous system was determined, showcasing the effectiveness of a specific performance indicator, also known as the $H_2$ norm in control theory. The study then explored the feasibility of achieving this optimal standard in a practical system, demonstrating the derivation of a precise discretization method that could be applied to this problem. The proposed solution involved using a simulation-based approach, specifically the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, to obtain numerical results and validate the discretization method's accuracy.

The Pierre Auger Observatory has discovered a pattern of significant year-to-year variations in the energy distribution of high-energy cosmic rays, particularly those with energies exceeding 4 EeV. This observation holds significant potential for uncovering unknown aspects of cosmic rays at these extreme energy levels. To aid in this endeavor, researchers will be provided with maps illustrating the temporal variations in cosmic ray data collected between 2016 and 2019.

Recently, several Zinbiel algebra analogues to well-known algebra structures like associative and Lie algebras have been identified. This research focuses on examining the fundamental properties of these specific types of algebras, in particular, the (3,)-associative variants. It is demonstrated through graphic extraction of the AZ-algebra intersection that all Zinbiel algebras3,5)=0 depict an empty set. Furthermore, numerous exclusive characteristics of the Zinbiel algebra structure are obtained.

A precise understanding of the initial state in heavy-ion collisions is crucial for interpreting the quark-gluon plasma's nearly perfect fluid behavior. To gain further insights, a new observable called the sideward flow angle is introduced to investigate event-by-event variations in reaction geometry. Our analysis of lead-lead collisions at the LHC reveals that the sideward flow angle is influenced by the number of participating nucleons and shows a correlation with the sideward fluctuation of the $v_2$ flow. Our findings are also influenced by experimental acceptance and finite-size effects. Furthermore, our study shows that the sideward fluctuation provides valuable information about the initial transverse geometry of the collision.

This research focuses on identifying and resolving inconsistencies in database tables, particularly those containing empty values. While previous work largely assumed complete data, we break this assumption and account for missing values treated as uncertain data. By integrating the concept of dependency frameworks, we define five types of inconsistencies caused by the violation of functional dependencies, then propose algorithms to detect and repair these issues. The validity of our approaches is demonstrated through experiments.

This research introduces a dynamic statistical model called the TV-POLR. PO autoregression is typically static, which limits its ability to forecast future data accurately. To address this forecast issue, PO time series models that can manage changing patterns were developed. Two methods, the gradual shift model and panel PO regression, constitute the PO time series framework and offer distinct advantages in flexibility and applicability. The gradual shift model is characterized by distinct parametric trends, whereas panel PO regression allows for individual-specific but constant parametric differences. Both methods are applied to real-world data sets, yielding improved forecast results compared to conventional PO regression. To facilitate larger scale applications, the research also provides variational inference algorithms for inferring unobserved variables and model parameters.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) for representing objects, which are fully parameterized by 12 degrees of freedom and provide a robust, invariant descriptor that excludes the need for a known object model. When a partial view of an object is observed from any angle, the corresponding NDF layer can be easily activated and applied to a downstream task. These layers are task-agnostic, promoting reusability, and are designed to be model-free, which enhances their applicability in dynamic settings. We evaluate NDFs in manipulation tasks, achieving a performance of 90% success in placing objects in a designated location without requiring prior object models. The source code is available online at this URL: https://github.com/jojojiang/Neural-Descriptor-Fields.

A key question in the study of statistical physics is whether the Yang-Lee edge singularity consistently appears at a specific point across all classical universality classes, characterized by the same critical exponents and amplitude ratios, regardless of their underlying length scale. Using a combination of high-precision numerical simulations through finite-size scaling and renormalization group analysis, we've determined the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity $x_{\rm c}$ near the origin for classical O(N) universality classes, including those describing uniaxial anisotropy (where $x$ represents anisotropy-induced fields), for various values of $N$ (1, 0.0064, 0.1428, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, and infinity). Our study also examines the validity of the square-root-scaling hypothesis for the Yang-Lee edge singularity position.

In statistics and machine learning, the challenge of denoising high-dimensional Gaussian data is addressed, with a focus on the TAP free energy's properties. To efficiently tackle the non-convornity of the local TAP landscape, an iterative algorithm with an expanded variable space is devised. This method succeeds in resolving the local TAP problem for a wide range of temperatures by extending the contraction range of the original Sudakov-Fernique argument. Additionally, an alternative, local-variational perspective is introduced, providing a new perspective on the tability of the TAP free energy. This in turn yields a concise proof of its local concavity. However, it's important to note that the local structure's influence on the TAP landscape remains unclear below a specific temperature threshold, beyond which the TAP free energy is variational and thus globally concave, as established in a preceding study.

The use of photometric data from amateur and automated amateur astronomers has significantly helped in monitoring atmospheric changes, including aerosols.  Aerometric data obtained via photometry requires fewer accurate instruments and can cover broader geographic areas than other methods, making it a valuable tool for aerometry.  This review examines recent progress in aerosol research using photometric data, covering retrieval techniques, validation with other measurement methods, and research on aerosol properties.  It also explores several research areas, including the development of retrieval algorithms, accounting for UV photometry, using machine learning, and collaborative efforts with organizations like Citizen Science.  It further discusses the use of data from automated cameras, including ground-based photometry systems, in aerometry.

Accurate 6D pose estimation is a crucial task in diverse applications like robotics and vision systems. Although effective 2D pose methods exist, they often struggle when applied to estimating poses in 3D space due to issues like pose variations and the lack of data annotation. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel approach called DeepHMap++, which transfers knowledge from a polynomial-based projection model to a fully convolutional network, adapting it for processing depth images. This adaptation involves two novel techniques: integrating projection grouping and a correspondence loss function. Our experiment shows that DeepHMap outperforms current regression methods on the KITTI dataset, achieving a significant improvement of 11.1% in accuracy, measured as the Average Pose Error.

Python is a widely used tool in statistical analysis that many researchers are familiar with.  GGLasso, the new Graphical Generalized Laplace Assumption module built in Python, extends the original Graphical Lasso functionality to handle Laplacian distributions and can process Generalized LP loss.  This module enables the computation of a probabilistic graph based on feature data, which is useful for various applications such as business.  Unlike the original Lasso approach that assumes Gaussian data, GGLasso is capable of managing real-world data sets, which often conform to power law distributions.  GGLasso relies on the Iterative Retree LP algorithm to efficiently solve for a positive definite graph.  The module contains several tests and demonstrates its applicability to real-world data sets.

A leading approach in constructing balance field-generating molecular structures involves molecular sampling from a specific probability distribution defined by the Lennard-Jones potential. This document explores the characteristics and properties of this distribution in detail, establishing its connection to Euler equations and proposing a method to compute the total energy conservation property of molecular samples. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the two distance metrics used in this context, resulting in a corrected, more robust distance metric. We also derive the optimal temperature parameter for the molecular dynamics Monte Carlo (MDMC) simulation, beyond which the energy conservation property becomes computationally significant. By leveraging these insights, we develop a novel, highly accurate method to sample molecules from the target distribution, which achieves the same statistical quality as the standard approach but with substantially lower computational costs. This new method also enables efficient computation of higher-order multipole moments and other relevant physical quantities. Moreover, we show the applicability of this approach to assessing the gravitational potential of complex structures, such as molecular chains and spheres composed of multiple molecules, with resulting sampling efficiencies improvements of up to two orders of magnitude compared to conventional methods.

As society's connectivity in the digital age spans multiple dimensions, network analysis has shifted from singular to multi-layered frameworks. 
To better characterize these complex, interconnected networks, our study develops a node prominence measure specifically tailored for multi-layered networks, building on the concept of node prominence first introduced by Contardo and colleagues in 2016. 
Our approach identifies nodes that stand out across individual network layers and serves as a standard for promoting freedom of expression online, using a real-world example based on Twitter's retweeting behavior around political events to demonstrate its effectiveness.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

When spheres move through fluids and hit surfaces, they can cause damage due to the forces involved. Understanding how spheres behave when they impact fluids and solid surfaces is important for preventing surface damage. This study focuses on a specific type of impact known as the "entry surface seal," where spheres become trapped in a thin film of fluid after impact. We investigated this phenomenon for various spheres impacting a air-filled cavity, considering different impact speeds and sphere sizes. Results show that the "entry surface seal" can lead to the spheres getting stuck, bursting the surface, or escaping, with different factors determining the outcome. Notable causes of sphere entrapment include the generation of pockets of low pressure that cause the surface to deform and eventually collapse, leading to the spheres becoming entraped. However, as impact velocity increases, the time it takes for pressure to build up behind the spheres decreases, causing the spheres to act like pistons and leading to rapid entrapment. This research provides new parameters and guidelines for understanding and accounting for sphere entrapment during surface impact.

A particular class of Type IIB orientifold theories with global symmetries that can be inferred from the arrangement of D-branes and orientifold planes in compactified Calabi-Yau four-folds is examined. By utilizing four-cycle operators within the Type IIB four-dimensional N=1 supergravity effective field theory, we examine possible extensions to the $\theta$-term's domain. These developments necessitate revising some of the theories' fundamental properties, particularly the axion shift symmetries and the associated anomaly.

The mineral cupricite, known as CuFe2S3, holds significant interest in the field of solid-state physics due to its rich composition of transition metals and unique structural characteristics that facilitate metal-to-insulator transitions. Previous studies on this material have primarily focused on individual transition metal sites, treating them independently as isolated systems. However, a comprehensive understanding requires considering the distinct electronic structures of each site. Through the use of local-density functional theory combined with an ensemble of Hubbard U methods, we conducted detailed investigations to examine inter-site interactions and determine the optimal treatment for each iron site. Our results show that ignoring inter-site interactions leads to misleading explanations of experimental data, whereas a approach that treats one iron site as localized and the other as itinerant provides the most consistent explanation of various physical properties. This material serves as an invaluable example showcasing the limitations of treating orbital-selective Mott phases and implies broader applications to other complex structures containing multiple transition metal atoms.

This research investigates the Rabi oscillations in a quantum system without an external magnetic field, where an exciton is swamped by coherent copies of itself undergoing Rabi flips. Rabi oscillations are typically linked to an external magnetic field, but in this study, they emerge from the coupling of an atom's electric dipole and magnetic octupole moments with strong artificial fields. Rabi frequency variations are demonstrated as the initial Rabi oscillation state and octupole transition probability are altered. The model incorporates the effects of Rabi oscillations on the absorption spectrum. Theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations of the Bloch equations, revealing Rabi splitting and asymmetric sidebands.

The electronic properties of two-dimensional (2D) hexagonal lattices are extensively studied due to their distinctive six-fold symmetry, yet this high degree of lattice symmetry constrines the modification of Dirac point locations. To address this limitation, we propose a lattice model for a four-fold symmetric triangular-triangular (TT) wallpaper lattice structure, capable of exhibiting Dirac points through spinless nearest-neighbor hopping. Through perturbation analysis and modeling, we demonstrate how hexagonal lattice attachments can be incorporated into TT structure lattices while preserving its unique non-symmorphic six-fold point group symmetry. By applying the Berry phase, we investigate the Hall effect in TT lattices and highlight their potential applications in Hall effect sensors and quantum interference effects. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of local on-site potentials on lattice structure, non-symmorphic hexagonal lattice structures, and suggest avenues for further exploration involving lattice modeling and spectroscopy.

Quantum states that possess a definite photon number, particularly when that number is one, are vital for securing coherent quantum technologies against phase errors. Achieving this level of coherence has been a significant technological challenge, and although it's theoretically possible to create such states directly, various experimental methods often produce a mix of different types of states, including quadrature-squeezed and Fock states. This technique, drawn from quantum-optical catalysis, can produce these states by using single photons to facilitate the interaction between counter-rotating non-linear resonators, and it's been demonstrated that this method yields perfectly pure single-photon facilitated coherent states with any desired intensity. However, as this technique relies on non-linear dispersion, it also comes with inherent limitations in terms of achieving an extremely narrow state.

Using the formalism of bivector basis in a real four-dimensional vector space, a comprehensive analysis of the Newman-Penrose framework in generalized relativity has been undertaken.  Initially, the basics of this approach were outlined before deriving the standard tetrad basis expressions.  This enables the direct transformation between the Newman-Penrose and Wu-Yau formulations.  Furthermore, by examining the Wu-Yau proof of the algebraic classification of the Weyl tensor, the algebraic properties of complex bivectors were explored.  Ultimately, the standard tetrad expression for the Weyl curvature tensor was obtained, providing a basis for exploring its application to the expression of the Petrov classification.

A new approach to identifying chemical formulas for polymers is presented, which tackles the complexity of traditional methods that struggle due to the lack of simple molecular units in many polymers. By applying graph theory to depict the structure of polymers, this method breaks them into composite molecular components, which are then used in a system of equations solved through linear optimization to preserve atomic integrity, coupled with an integer optimization to determine stoichiometric coefficients, which can be verified against existing data. This approach is effectively demonstrated using three distinct polymer examples, which also serves to highlight the limitations of conventional methods.

Segmenting tumors in the esophagus using computed tomography images is still a challenging task due to the presence of difficult-to-segment parts, such as those with low contrast, irregular borders, and discontinuous structures. This study presents a novel deep learning model, DDAUnet, to improve the segmentation of esophageal tumors. DDAUnet is based on a variant of the U-Net architecture and integrates three key components: dense connections, atrous convolution, and attention mechanisms. DDAUnet draws on dense connections to share information effectively between network modules, thus reducing the model's parameters while enhancing its representation capabilities. This allows DDAUnet to handle complex and discontinuous tumor structures. To handle difficult-to-segment parts of the tumor, DDAUnet employs atrous components to expand its receptive field without losing resolution. This helps to capture long-range dependencies in the data. To focus on relevant regions, DDAUnet uses an attention mechanism to allocate more resources to areas of the tumor that are difficult to segment. To evaluate the DDAUnet model, we used a dataset of 109 CT images with segmented tumors in the esophagus, and compared it with other state-of-the-art network architectures, including UNet, 3D UNet, D-UNet, Atrous Unet, and AttUnet. Multilingual individuals often switch between languages when communicating, known as code-switching or code-mixing, which can create barriers to adopting new technologies due to the lack of comprehensive language support technologies. To address this issue, researchers aim to develop robust language models that cover multiple languages, but this goal is hindered by various challenges including limited data, imbalanced language distribution, and lack of metadata about the mixed content. To overcome these obstacles and advance the field, it is crucial to study mixed-language data, conduct experiments, and gain a deeper understanding of the underlying social factors that influence multilingual communication. To facilitate this progress, the authors propose an open-access dataset called MIMICO, along with carefully selected examples and research questions to guide future studies in this emerging field.

As multiple human-to-human description generation systems are being released, it's human reference information now being used to evaluate automated descriptions that should be explored. We're presenting a framework for utilizing human reference descriptions, which are typically not structured, to evaluate automated image descriptions. This framework involves utilizing a set of structured descriptions to establish a connection with the unstructured descriptions produced by humans. It's shown through evaluations on the Facebook AI caption dataset and MS COCO captions' subset, to effectively assess automated descriptions, this framework works. Additionally, key factors are identified as making certain unstructured descriptions from humans more valuable in the absence of which, their utility is limited.

To understand the underlying causes of its complex structure, ta2O5 ground state crystal forms were investigated using advanced simulation techniques. Nine distinct Ta2O5 phase structures were identified, but none matched the characteristics required for electrical conductivity. These features included various ta2O5 phase classifications, and corresponding electronic properties were also analyzed. Ta2O5 phase classifications included tao5-γ, nawrocki, nawrocki-10Gd2O3, nawrocki-Y2O3, nawrocki-Ce2O3, nawrocki-Nd2O3, nawrocki-Sm2O3, nawrocki-Gd2O3, and an unknown Ta2O5 phase. Ta2O5 phase structures required specific space groups and coordination numbers for accurate identification. To determine the Ta2O5 ground state structure, simulated O2 pressures were applied to each phase, but none produced the necessary features. Instead, an energy-constrained Ta2O5 structure was discovered with octahedral coordination for Ta2O5 atoms in a specific space group. However, this phase transformed into an insulating state under simulated conditions. Previous studies demonstrated that the Big Geographic Sort (BGS) feature on Reddit can amplify the spread of false information by encouraging users to share content based on their region's significance rather than their personal values. Our research builds upon this by examining specific aspects of the BGS that were not previously analyzed. We focus on two key issues: (a) the connection between BGS and the dissemination of misinformation stemming from content that is not inherently values-based, and (b) the relationship between the demographics of a subreddit and the BGS' capacity to accelerate the spread of false information. Our data comes from Reddit users' interactions with a manipulated news article posted to five highly populated subreddits. Our findings suggest that the BGS leads users to share content in order to signal their affiliation with important places, in this instance, however, the BGS did not cause the spread of misinformation. Our study further reveals that the impact of the BGS on content sharing varies depending on the Subreddit's demographics, in this instance, older and more female users tended to share content more frequently. Our study contributes to the growing body of work on the BGS' effects and provides valuable insights for content moderators and the designers of algorithms that rank content.

Verbal guidance from human instructors plays a significant role in the successful execution of complex tasks by robots, especially when working together on cooperative projects. To effectively assist humans, robots need a solid understanding of the verbal explanations provided by their instructors. This research focuses specifically on social explanations, in which instructors share their thoughts with the robot, in order to develop a more cooperative relationship. However, to achieve this, a solid foundation for analyzing these explanations is essential. Unfortunately, such a base does not currently exist. In this work, we investigate and compare various explanation patterns used by instructors who have demonstrated tasks to a robot. Our analysis reveals that the content of the explanations varies greatly among instructors but remains consistent for the same instructor across different tasks. This finding supports the possibility of a universal model capable of capturing explanation patterns by training on data from just one instructor. Our hypotheses have been validated through experiments, paving the way for a unified framework to analyze and leverage explanation patterns in robot learning applications.

By applying the principles of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras and their associated conformal structures, we have re-derived key aspects of 2d central charge $c$ CFT intricacy, specifically its intricate tensor structure and tensor shadow properties. Within this research, complex tensor interplay is described mathematically as the "tensor bracket," a modified version of the native bracket that results from the infinite-dimensional Lie algebra's association with a specific vector space.

The evaluation of conversational systems has been undertaken by both human assessors and automated methods, which include the use of simple bots for basic systems and sophisticated Debatte tests for sophisticated ones. Introducing a novel framework, we present a systematic approach to assessing a range of conversational systems, from simpler to more advanced versions, based on a unified testing system. This framework utilizes fundamental test components that can be combined to create various test suites. A distinctive feature of our approach is the use of automated testers to conduct evaluations. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through the assessment of a range of conversational systems, including the Open Assistant, a multi-turn web-based assistant, and the Small Talk bot.

The exploration of conic expressions within the Julia programming language is presented, specifically using a third-generation conic solver suite in Julia known as Hypatia.jl, which comprises three packages: SeDuji, JuMP, and a specific conic solver. This paper examines natural outcomes when employing HOSR expressions with the SeDuji package and proposes solutions to address related issues. The study is demonstrated through various applications within the Julia programming language, drawing insights from mathematical theory and optimizer behavior.

The rapid development of advanced MRI techniques and deep learning models has significantly improved the diagnosis of neurological disorders, but this progress also highlights the need for efficient quality control methods. The incorporation of learned constraints into the reconstruction process has been a successful strategy, yet this also stresses the importance of reliable automated quality assurance. We examined the performance of existing MRI quality assurance methods across 10 different protocols and found that they generally failed to generalize well to new data due to protocol-specific overfitting. Our research demonstrated that simple generalization approaches, such as training on diverse protocols, could improve the effectiveness of current state-of-the-art methods. However, this also generalizes the impact of protocol-specific overfitting, showing that even the most effective models struggle to accurately identify defective scans without personalized training. This in turn suggests that the use of learned quality assurance models on new protocols may be limited, presenting both a challenge and an opportunity to develop more reliable quality control methods in MRI.

This study investigates how private electric car owners' behavior impacts the ability of distribution networks to bounce back from disruptions. By using multi-agent simulation and optimization, we've developed a platform to balance the costs of charging during outages and give up using the grid when alternative charging options are limited. In order to manage the vast number of decision variables, a cost function minimization approach has been employed. Furthermore, this study derives the relationship between charging costs and outages, offering insights into strategic cost management. Numerical results provide concrete examples of how this relationship changes and offers advice on setting charging limits to reduce costs while limiting the effect on the environment. Finally, we've shown that resilient operation costs can be significantly higher than non-resilient ones, with a ratio of up to 10 times the original costs.

In this study, we tackle the challenging problem of multi-agent recurrent encounters between the same partners, which has significant applications in areas like sales, real estate transactions, and negotiations. To address this issue, we propose a recurrent drive incentive mechanism that encourages agents to meet repeatedly by fostering an intrinsic desire to resolve their ongoing curiosity. Our theoretical analysis and compelling simulation experiments reveal that our model successfully captures the essence of recurrent encounters. Notably, our model requires very little learning time for agents to grasp the necessary behavior.

This study employs an ab initio approach using the full-potential augmented plane wave plus local orbitals method to investigate the structural, electronic and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds. We investigated the effect of different crystallographic phases of Gd and Cm on the results. All phases were found to adopt the Fe3Sn2 structure type with space group $D^{12}_{3d}$ (164). Our findings reveal that all compounds exhibit indirect band gaps with values of approximately 0.5 eV. Notably, both GdSn3 and CmSn3 display half-metallic behavior for all considered phases, with 100% spin-polarized conductivity channels. The magnetization values for GdSn3 range from 6.55 to 7.66 T, while those for CmSn3 range from 0.55 to 4.16 T. Furthermore, the exchange splittings for all phases of GdSn3 and CmSn3 are located at the M-K high-symmetry points in the Brillouin zone. The GdSn3 compound exhibits ferromagnetic ordering in all considered phases, while CmSn3 exhibits various magnetic orderings with corresponding energies. The GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds were found to be mixtures of the constituent phases of GdSn3 and CmSn3.

Predictions for the number of extra baryons and mesons are presented for various
early universe scenarios. The fraction of extra baryons and mesons is predicted
to be approximately $10^{-16}$ times the photon population for quark–gluon plasma,
and about $10^{-14}$ for both quark matter and pion matter. These estimates are
given as functions of the baryon asymmetry and the temperature of the universe.
Additionally, the absolute population of extra baryons and mesons is plotted
against the temperature of the universe for several early universe models.

For any finite reflection group, the "foundation theorem" establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the simple reflections and the fundamental (or unknotted) link patterns. For a specific subset of these groups, the "fundamental set" is defined as the collection of link patterns that represent the simplest, or trivial, group elements through the partial braid group. While a refined approach to reflexive transitive relations recently allowed for a deeper understanding of the structure of this set for the symmetric group, this research generalizes that proof method to include the P$_{n}$ and S$_{n}$-subgroups of the partial symmetric group. Consequently, this provides a more intuitive insight into the abelian nature of these specific group subsets.

While gravitational lensing effects in the context of the Pantheon dataset are well understood, a puzzling phenomenon was recently pointed out by huto_2020, suggesting that a significant majority of Type Ia supernovae produce insufficient feedback to escape their host galaxies. This issue arises from an assumption that may not hold true for all scenarios, as it ignores the possibility of moving masses creating a Doppler shift that confounds measurements of gravitational lensing when observing distant light. To address this challenge, a simple model was developed to estimate the magnitude of light from Type Ia supernovae while accounting for their high velocities relative to their host galaxies. Notably, these effects can be as significant as 10 percent in certain cases, either in terms of brightness or angular size, and can even result in anti-lensing phenomena that lead to substantial feedback, thus helping to explain the data presented by huto_2020.

Photonic structures have been developed to incorporate T-shaped bends with minimal loss, using a novel method based on symmetry preservation. By carefully designing the bends so that mirror symmetry is maintained through the vertical stem, nearly extrinsic scatterings are minimized, according to time-independent Schrodinger's scatterings rules. This approach enables high-performance T-junctions and bends with minimal scatterings, essential for integrating compact and efficient photonic circuits, crucial for quantum information processing and other applications, on silicon-based platforms.

Our study contrasts our object encodings approach with the background context encodings used by Rahn et al. (2018) to evaluate the impact of incorporating contextual information in object recognition by a system. Our findings show that although context provides an advantage in straightforward scenarios, our deep trained object encoder excels even without contextual information.

This research investigates a highly complex system of differential equations, categorized as a "no net letter" type, which contains singular terms and an interplay of functions that follow a specific mathematical growth pattern. The equation system, coupled with zero boundary conditions, is studied, and conditions are established to ensure the existence of solutions. In seeking these conditions, distinct scenarios are identified and thoroughly analyzed, each offering distinct mathematical insights and implications.

To develop improved guarantees for GDM samplers in robust mean estimation, it's essential to understand the concentration properties of sums of binary variables that exhibit negative correlation. Our study provides refined drift bounds specifically tailored to two-binary-variable negatively correlated random processes. Moreover, we examine four major variants of negative correlation, demonstrating how each relates to one another and ultimately converges to the same framework. As a practical application, we investigate the correlations inherent in GDM samples and determine that they possess strong forms of negative correlation, ultimately enabling us to derive the same concentration inequalities.

Lebesgue's technique in integrating certain non-Riemann-integrable functions involved creating a measure that matched the target function on a majority of the domain. This concept can be linked to repairing a function to make it integrable. In the context of symplectic geometry, we introduce the term "symplectic alteration" to describe transforming a symplectic manifold into another while maintaining equivalence under symplectic isotopy. We define two methods for incorporating points into a manifold in accordance with the target symplectic structure. Additionally, we introduce the concept of "acceptable isotopy," a variant of homotopy that allows for temporary departures from the intended isotopy, as long as the starting and ending configurations are considered equivalent. We demonstrate that the results of incorporating points are unaffected by the method used, as long as the process is carried out via the same isotopy type, effectively establishing the starting and ending configurations as being equivalent under symplectic algebraic type.

Transplanting kidneys that are incompatible with the recipient often faces higher acceptance limits than suitable kidneys, yet the underlying原因 remains unclear. We conducted a survey with 42 transplant nephrologists to assess their ideal acceptance compatibility. Our results indicate that the average ideal compatibility interval is [45%, 70%], with 95% confidence. Compatible kidneys show 85% of the population and indicate they are equally indifferent between rejecting an incompatible kidney and waiting for a suitable one. The compatibility interval's midpoint aligns with the 75th and 91st percentiles of the usual acceptance range. This suggests that, ideally, compatibility should play a more significant role in determining which patients receive incompatible kidneys and that the current practice of accepting most patients may be overly broad.

This study investigates the capacity of deep learning-based word representations to grasp the semantic meaning of financial sentiment, specifically the Loughran-McDonald sentiment dictionary. Our findings reveal that traditional representation methods, including SVD, can effectively capture the semantic relationships within the sentiment dictionary, with positive words clustering together and negative words exhibiting opposite spatial orientations. However, it's crucial to note that these clustering patterns are more likely a reflection of the frequency of the words in the training data, rather than an indication of their semantic understanding. Despite this finding, we believe that deep learning-based sentiment analysis remains a valuable tool for analyzing the emotional content of financial texts.

This work introduces SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based wideband signal processing frameworks for simultaneous data and power transmission, called SISO-OFDM-IPT and MISO-OFDM-IPT respectively. These frameworks are derived from the primary IQR interface information feedback constraints, mirating the initial innovations presented in our prior paper at NBS. In contrast to multiple antennas and multiple carriers, where extra performance gains are not guaranteed, this work investigates the conditions and strategies for simultaneously achieving high data rates and efficiency in IPT using OFDM-based waveforms in communication systems with mobile data terminals capable of IPT functions. It is demonstrated that by strategically selecting subcarriers for IPT in both SISO and MISO environments, additional performance can be gained beyond what multiple antennas and multiple carriers provide, with suboptimal greedy algorithms presented to achieve this by integrating power for data transmission and IPT into a single calculation. Through extensive simulations, it is shown that the extra benefit of integrated power transmission is significant, with the extra gain of multiple carriers being comparable to multiple antennas in certain scenarios.

This study introduces an approach combining the level-set method with an embedded boundary technique to accurately model the physics of solidification and melting. 
Our implementation integrates a level-set method within a finite volume framework for an embedded boundary, enabling efficient numerical computation. 
To further optimize performance, we developed a semi-implement-independent solver that leverages the benefits of GPU acceleration. 
This researcher was able to produce high-resolution simulations with excellent conservation properties and a stable interface capillary number of 0.1. 
Our approach demonstrated the ability to accurately replicate both the Thomas-Fermi problem's temperature distribution and the thermodynamic cycle, as well as handle more intricate scenarios such as Rayleigh-B\'enard and Stefan problems with oscillating interfaces. 
This solver achieved high performance, reaching a peak of 49.669 $\times$ 10$^6$ operations per second per GPU in a 64-GPU configuration with an interface Reynolds number of 1000.

In the context of multi-player games, we introduce a learning mechanism that utilizes rationalizability to converge on equilibrium strategies. This approach adapts the conventional best-response dynamics by incorporating exploration and noise, enabling it to discover and stabilize on the rationalizable equilibrium of games with continuous action spaces and payoff structures for players. Notably, this learning algorithm is algorithmically straightforward, and it is capable of finding the rationalizable equilibrium of all normal-form games in both unopposed and multi-player competitive settings with the number of actions limited to a finite set.

The reliability of complex networks is significantly compromised by the spread of failures, also known as cascades. These phenomena occur when failures propagate through interconnected networks and can lead to widespread system breakdowns. Given the potential for catastrophic consequences, understanding and mitigating cascade risks has gained considerable attention in recent years. Until now, most studies on cascade risks have focused on cases where a failing node loses all its connections. However, real-world scenarios often involve the loss of only some connections, a situation that requires a more nuanced approach. To address this, a novel mathematical framework is proposed, incorporating preventive network restructuring to seal broken connections and avert complete system failure. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, the impact of this approach on two well-established cascade models is demonstrated, with the possibility of containing cascade failures to minimal proportions.

Fits to determine the parton distribution functions (PDFs) within hadrons are integral to particle physics experiments. To achieve this, theoretical frameworks are employed to interpret measured quantities in relation to the PDFs. While established frameworks facilitate the interpretation of hard processes based on their connection to the hard scattering cross section, processes with a soft component present additional challenges. To address processes with final state radiation, recombination, or absorption, frameworks like PYTHIA 8, HERWIG++ with LEPOSWD, and POWIGLAP are utilized. Furthermore, direct processes involving heavy quarks in the hadron can fit only when accounting for the quark PDF within the hadron. To determine this, global PDF fits are conducted to extract the heavy quark PDF from the data.

Reinforcement learning algorithms often incorporate experience replay to boost both their efficiency and performance. However, there's an underlying assumption in these methods that experiences are sampled independently, which isn't consistently met in situations involving policy-based experience replay. In this work, we introduce a theory that investigates the variance of the total experience collected by an agent, accounting for the dependence between sampled experiences. We then utilize this framework to develop two novel policies for managing the size of the experience buffer: one that modifies the experience sampling method and another that adjusts the buffer's capacity. These policies are designed to minimize experience overlap and consequently reduce the variance of the collected data. To demonstrate the benefits of our approach, we conduct numerical simulations and apply our algorithms to the problem of curriculum learning in a real-world scenario, showing that our methods outperform the standard experience replay technique.

In our analysis of contemporary human conversations, we've identified a series of complex decision points that lead to exponentially growing conversation pathways. To accommodate these choices and testing requirements, we've developed the MultiTalk framework, capable of generating and evaluating discussions that involve multiple participants. This allows for more realistic conversation scenarios, complete with interruptions, abrupt topic shifts, and speakers taking over from one another. By utilizing the MultiTalk dataset, we've been able to facilitate conversations among three agents, spanning a wide range of topics and styles. This has proven valuable for research into the evaluation of sophisticated, face-to-face interactions among several people, with our findings showing that continuous, ununplanned conversations can lead to rapidly expanding possibilities, with just ten decision points allowing for nearly 1,300 different sequences.

We created N-body simulation codes to replicate the results of general-cosmological gravity theories by simulating the formation of structures in a rapidly N-body manner. These codes, based on linear perturbation theory, approximate the formation of structures with high precision, matching those produced by realistic simulations. For efficiency, these N-body simulations are significantly faster than their realistic counterparts, allowing for a large parameter space to be explored in a short amount of time. However, their validity is limited to a narrow range of scales and for less densely formed structures. Two code variants were produced, one continuous and one discrete, to simulate a specific type of gravitational theory, f(R). This demonstration shows that more complex models can be simulated for the first time in a computationally feasible manner, but also highlights the importance of not relying solely on N-body simulations for F(R) models due to non-separable equations. Despite their limitations, these simulations provide a valuable framework for large-scale simulations of a wide range of gravitational models, provided their validity is carefully considered.

We establish that in the complex plane, conditioned Gaussian free fields can serve as natural boundaries for an infinite family of simultaneously evolving Schramm-Loewner differential equations. This framework allows us to develop time-dependent versions of SLE and provide a stochastic partial differential equation description of the SLE evolution. Moreover, by leveraging this theory, we are able to interpret the Dyson's Brownian motion analogue as a system of SLEs and resolve certain outstanding problems regarding the interaction parameters in SLEs.

Researchers who utilize version control systems and collaborative editing platforms like GitHub and MediaWiki have successfully combined these tools to create highly effective collective projects. Despite the benefits of using MediaWiki for teamwork, its underdeveloped automatic version control features have limited its usage in collective research endeavors. This study introduces a customized version of MediaWiki called WorkingWiki, which integrates the original system's capabilities with those of Git, to facilitate a more functional and efficient collective research project. By examining a real-world application, we demonstrate that using WorkingWiki can support successful collective research efforts.

This research focuses on modeling the complex interaction between a turbulent jet fire and acoustic forces within a linearized framework, addressing the limitations of fully nonlinear simulations and experimental settings. A novel active flame technique was employed to apply localized perturbations to a flame and its turbulent fluctuations, based on a linearized reaction model. Although this approach has previously been used for surface instability problems, its application to internal flow phenomena appears to be new. Despite the constraints of the linearized framework, the study successfully captures key features of the thermoacoustic instability, allowing for an efficient investigation of parametric influences on instability development. Analysis of the flow's response to forcing reveals the presence of a primary resonance within the jet pipe and the impact of key factors including Mach number, area ratio, and Reynolds number on instability development.

We investigate the potential for ultralight dark matter in the form of scalar particles that interact with neutrinos, shaping neutrino mass and neutrinoless double beta decay parameters. Utilizing neutrino oscillation data, cosmological observations, and neutrinoless double beta decay measurements as constraints, we assess the theory's viability. Unless the coupling constant exceeds 10^{-9}, a viable parameter space exists, with a predicted density of neutrinos within the required range and a massless neutrino oscillation pattern. In this scenario, the theory predicts a specific probability for neutrinoless double beta decay. Conversely, if the neutrinos are given a major minussuppressed mass pattern, the theoretical framework results in a very low predicted probability for neutrinoless double beta decay. Additionally, if the theory is valid, we expect a time-varying amplitude of neutrinoless double beta decay as it is affected by the oscillating dark matter. However, current experiments are not sensitive enough to detect this effect.

Nonlocal gravity theory proposes a nonperturbative reformation of quantum general relativity by expanding gravity theories based on a non-differentiable connection. This paper explores two examples of nonlocal gravity theories, Mirza-Kosteleck\'y (NK) and Hendrickson-Kosteleck\'y (HK), and highlights the importance of an induced connection, which is non-perturbative in the cosmological constant, as a fundamental element of the theory. By treating the induced connection and the tetrad field as independent and fundamental, the theorems of Poincar\'e and Gauss are applied to the the induced connection. Applying the theorems of de Rham cohomology to the the induced connection shows that the theorems of Poincar\'e and Gauss are independent and provide a the induced connection that is solved in terms of the tetrad field. This result allows the nonlocal gravity theories to be rewritten in the the Einstein-Hilbert action, demonstrating that the the induced connection, the tetrad field can be solved in terms of the the induced connection, providing a consistent classical theory. The theorems of Poincar\'e and Gauss are shown to be crucial to the consistency of the nonlocal gravity theories. As large-scale sequencing continues for thousands of individuals, the association signals identified in genome-wide association studies are increasingly being refined by integrating functional genomic data. We assessed how effective various annotation sources are at re-ranking randomly selected null loci from across the human genome, using 18 traits from the UK Biobank as examples. We examined three main categories of functional annotations: those identifying accessibly accessible regions, those pinpointing evidence of function based on evolutionary and biochemical analyses, and the integration of multiple accessibly accessible biologic processes. We also compared different methods of combining multiple biologic process scores. We found that focusing on accessible regions provides only a Rejection Rate of 11%, whereas using expression quantitative trait loci information achieves 21%. The most successful category, using combined biologic process scores, resulted in average rejection rates of 31%. Furthermore, utilizing a logistic regression model to prioritize peaks yielded the best outcomes with a average rank of 15th, followed by composite scoring methods with a average rank of 17th.

This paper explores the current state of research on small systems produced at the LHC, focusing on experiments with high-energy photons, electrons, and muons produced in deep inelastic scattering (DIS) and single photon production. These(DIS) and single photon production processes serve as "reverse probes" to study the initial state of these small systems. We review the state of the art in this field, highlighting significant challenges in understanding small systems, such as flow and particle production at low transverse momentum. We also discuss relevant theoretical approaches, including color glass condensate effective field theory and hybrid renormalization group evolution, to better understand these small systems.

The orbital decay of neutron star X-ray binaries in the Milky Way's center is linked to the recurrence time of their outbursts through a specific relationship established by Jayanti and Janssen in a 2021 study. This study aims to validate this relationship by analyzing the recurrence periods of nine prominent outbursts from neutron stars in the Milky Way's center, including X-ray novae, Type C storms, and barium stars. Initially, calculating the orbital decay times for these nine stars becomes challenging due to the lack of precise mass estimates for each star. To work around this obstacle, we assume the recurrence periods of these stars are determined by the transfer of disk accretion, allowing us to estimate their masses based on typical values of mass accretion rates found in previous research. Consequently, a general agreement is found between calculated and measured recurrence periods for the majority of the stars, with exceptions being GX.3-1 and GX.5-1 which exhibit longer recurrence periods than expected. This study also explores the characteristics of GX.3-1 and GX.5-1 in comparison to other quiescent X-ray stars in the Milky Way's center, finding that they share similar properties but differ from stars exhibiting faster thermal evolution. This distinction may suggest that GX.3-1 and GX.5-1 have unique features setting them apart from other quiescent X-ray stars in the Milky Way's center.

Based on a simple harmonic oscillator model, we examine the coupled spin, vibration, and electron systems under the influence of inertial forces caused by linear acceleration. To fill the gap in current knowledge, we derive the fundamental equations for combined invariance and propose new terms in the Hamiltonian to account for electron-induced atomic displacement and the modulation of spin vibration frequencies. Our analysis reveals that: (i) the acceleration-induced Coriolis force can modulate vibration frequencies and cause electron deformation through changes in the vibration potential; (ii) the inertial force can cause a permanent electron deformation and displacement of the equilibrium harmonic state; and (iii) the fluctuation of the spin magnetic field can induce additional atomic displacement and vibration-induced electromagnetism that is insensitive to time-reversal and parity invariance. These effects, although generally weak, can be more significant in highly sensitive measurement scenarios or micro/nano devices with reduced inertia, and have the potential to lead to novel applications and fundamental understanding.

Stein's semantic variety measure effectively identifies individual differences in meaning between conversations, building on the Natural Language Understanding (NLU) task of Natural Language Inference (NLI). We introduce a new dataset, the Multi-turn Natural Language Inference (MuNLI), which extends the MuNLI data by adding semantic variety annotations for each speaker. In experiments, our models successfully predict semantic variety across conversations using NLI-based representations, outperforming previous methods that relied solely on text, by an average of 14.3 points, highlighting the importance of M-NLU in understanding human conversation.

The stability and evolution of young, rotating sub-stellar bodies in the early phases after their formation is influenced by a combination of rotation, fluid dynamics, and radiation physics. To understand the physics governing these objects, a computational modeling approach using SPHROT was employed, enabling the investigation of structure, temperature distribution, surface emission, and the effects of rapid rotation on object integrity. As the rotation rate increases, centrifugal force causes the distribution of mass to become elongated in the direction of rotation, resulting in the development of oblate shapes. Unlike spherical objects, the structure of rotating sub-stellar bodies has two distinct size measures: the radius at the center of rotation and the minimum distance required to enclose the object. Objects can lose mass through the shedding of material when the minimum distance becomes unreachable, but mass held tightly by rotation is protected from tidal forces exerted by nearby objects. The modeling results indicate that objects can reach a point of breakup due to rotation, despite having high rates of spin rotation. The modeling findings can be applied to the analysis of object radii, object collisions, and the capture of objects through gravitational forces.

To improve support for amplitude estimation frameworks with their capability to incorporate influential systematic errors, this paper proposes a straightforward and versatile technique to represent the ALICE's radial flow measurements in $s$- and $p$-Ts using parametrized flow coefficients within they evaluated models. In addition, it compares two alternative methods to process the ALICE's error structures, namely, convolution and covariance matrix incorporation, through a case study on charmonium resonances in $p$-T at $\sqrt{s} = 3.8$ GeV for $ \bar{p} $-N collisions at 8 GeV. The results show that convolution effectively handles the ALICE's non-Gaussian distributions, although incorporating the covariance matrix yields marginal improvements. Furthermore, this study also examines the ALICE's reported systematic errors, finding that ignoring the systematic flow evaluations beyond additive approaches leads to underestimation of the total systematic uncertainties, especially at high transverse momenta.

A distinctive outburst in X-ray radiation from space, known as GRB-Afterglow, provides critical information about the initial event. A novel theory has been developed to explain the early radiation, an external shockwave, and its connection to charged particles. This new approach, based on detailed mathematical analysis, has led to the prediction of specific patterns of light, allowing for the exploration of complex physical phenomena, including interactions with gas and magnetic fields, and the effects of extremely high temperatures on space. However, the model's assumptions may not fully explain all observed effects, and further research is needed to develop more comprehensive theories that incorporate the vast ranges of radiation and long-lasting effects on the surrounding environment.

A key question in parameterized complexity theory asks whether a problem can be solved by breaking down the input based on a given parameter, in this case, a problem's parameter's influence on the solution is analyzed. A prominent subfield of research focuses on problems that can be solved with a runtime of $f(k)$, where $k$ is the parameter and this research aims to prove that for any graph with a specific property and a parameter, the graph can be divided into two sets with given sizes in polynomial time. A specific example of this property is a graph being $H$-free, where $H$ is itself a specific subgraph with a given parameter. A specific application of this result is shown for finding a subgraph with given properties and a subgraph with a given parameter.

This research focuses on developing a novel, fully actuated leg that is both efficient and robust for bipedal robots. To achieve this, we propose a leg design featuring a high-pressure air piston to drive a swing-style movement. By utilizing stored air pressure, the need for multiple joints and numerous actuators can be eliminated, allowing the piston to lift the entire leg assembly. This design is intended for applications involving the transportation of fluids or fluids under pressure. A complete, two-legged robot is modeled in simulation, demonstrating the leg's capability to execute complex tasks like climbing and carrying cargo. In comparisons with a conventional spur-style leg, the piston-driven leg shows superior lifting power. In addition, the study outlines methods for attaching these legs to a two-legged robot and for controlling its movement, with simulations showing coordinated, efficient, and surprisingly agile motion.
