This research focuses on developing a sophisticated approach to detect skin lesions, ranging from benign moles to malignant melanoma, which is the most fatal form of skin cancer. To achieve this, we utilize a deep learning algorithm, specifically a Residual Neural Network, to analyze over 4,500 dermoscopic images. In addition to examining various image characteristics, we incorporate an outlier detection method based on entropy to identify and give extra weight to atypical samples. Through our evaluation, we show that this entropy-based approach successfully distinguishes between difficult-to-tell apart image types and enhances the overall accuracy of the classification model.

A spinning Hele-Shaw cell containing a viscous fluid is the subject of this study, where a less dense fluid is then injected through a central spindle. Instabilities arise as the injected fluid spreads, resulting in a fingers that form at the interface between the two fluids. The spinning cell induces orbital instability, causing these interface-generated structures to bend and curve. The injected fluid typically creates a primary stem as it overcomes surface tension, which in turn induces the formation of closed loops behind it. The STEM technique was used to obtain precise measurements of stem width and loop size. The research reveals that in this dynamic setting, torsion, rather than being intrinsically present, can be quantifiable and measured, with implications for understanding complex fluid behaviors.

A strikingly low hydrogen/helium ratio in interstellar space has been reported, and this discovery has prompted researchers to reexamine the conditions necessary for their occurrence. This reevaluation has been facilitated by the identification of two previously unknown compounds, ethynyl cyclopentadiene and diethynyl cyclopentadiene, in the TMC-1 molecular cloud, whose cyclopentadiene backbones have been confirmed through the detection of their characteristic rotational spectra. Notably, the presence of these compounds with complex, cyclic structures contradicts the expected prevalence of simple interstellar hydrogen compounds, and as a result, the conditions for their existence remain enigmatic. Unfortunately, the conditions for the formation of these compounds remain unknown, and as a result, the relevance of this discovery to the broader interstellar community has been limited. However, the indirect implication that a third element must have been present to compensate for the missing hydrogen has been apparent, and as a result, the relevance of this discovery to the interstellar community has been apparent. Notably, the presence of scandium in the TMC-1 molecular cloud has been confirmed, and as a result, the indirect implication that the hydrogen/helium ratio in interstellar space is significantly lower than previously believed has been confirmed.

Neural machine translation(NMT) models have achieved substantial success, yet they fall behind rule-based methods in translating certain structures with extended dependencies. To bridge this gap, incorporating prior knowledge into NMT frameworks has been proposed. We introduce a novel attention mechanism, known as Look-Forward Attention, that utilizes additional context - specifically, the subsequent word's information, which is largely unavailable during NMT generation due its autoregressive nature. We validate the effectiveness of our model through empirical experiments and demonstrate its practical advantage over standard NMT with attention, by incorporating a simple yet effective prior without utilizing extended training data. The robustness of our model is further confirmed through ablation studies on various NMT architectures and parameter settings. We also explore the relationship between Look-Forward Attention and Standard Attention, revealing a strong correlation and providing theoretical underpinnings. Furthermore, an analysis of the learned Look-Forward Attention weights, along with the associations between attention weights and word embeddings, offers valuable insights into the operational dynamics of NMT models during word generation. We believe the findings of this study are valuable for the NMT community and that our model's straightforward design holds potential for real-world applications.

The framework approach to software engineering is widely regarded as effective, yet its successful application remains elusive for many practitioners. This presentation will examine how a framework was transferred to a new context to develop the Grid Software Framework (GSF). We began with an existing open-source object-oriented method framework and adapted it for a non-object-oriented setting. This process involved changing the syntax to C and adding makefiles to automate code generation. The resulting modified framework was tested with a small grid computing project, which led to the decision to expand and refine it. Over time, this version of the framework was further developed into GSF through integration of new features, which were generated automatically. The objects and relationships within the framework were found to be sufficiently flexible to support the necessary functionality, thus eliminating the need to rewrite the framework in its entirety. This case study highlights the effectiveness of using a translated framework approach in a complex software development project.

A new, non-equivalent version of the combined dark fluid model is proposed, which incorporates a dissipative mechanism to address the stability issues encountered in previous formulations during the matter-dominated era. In this model, the matter component adheres to a density proportionality to the cube of the scale factor, while the non-Boltzmann matter component is proportional to the two-fifths power of the density. Through direct solutions of the Friedmann equations in a flat universe, it is demonstrated that matter-dominated eras are invariably inconsistent regardless of whether the Hubble parameter is positive or negative. However, it is also shown that cosmic expansion can be sustained indefinitely, provided the density of the non-Boltzmann matter component is sufficiently constrained. Conversely, if this constraint is not met, a point of singularity is formed, which is a result that remains the same for both positive and negative Hubble parameter scenarios. By applying this model to a specific galaxy, it is found that the combined dark fluid could be accounted for by combinations of cold dark matter and dark energy, in either order, thus demonstrating its equivalence to $\Lambda$CDM on an individual galaxy level.

This research investigates the implications of the unidentified neutrino and dark energy within the framework of effective field theory, suggesting that $J/\psi$ decays into visible and invisible components can provide lower bounds on interaction scales.  By analyzing visible modes, specifically a, gS, and Z bosons produced in these decays, we establish that there is no limit on the interaction scale for the effective field theory of the neutrino.  However, it is found that dark energy scales must be exceedingly small, ranging between $10^{-22}$ and $10^{-27}$, which is an extremely restrictive condition.  From past experiments on missing energy, similar but wider bounds on dark energy are derived, resulting in scales between $10^{-19}$ and $10^{-24}$.  In contrast, from future facilities such as Belle II and BESIII, more stringent boundaries can be set based on measurements of the missing decay rate of $J/\psi$, which, if observed with a branching ratio of $10^{-5}$, would imply that the neutrino is active.  Otherwise, with current data, similar to the limits established from the missing decay of $\tau$ leptons, very small scales for the effective field theory of the dark sector are set, specifically between $10^{-38}$ and $10^{-43}$.

Multivariate functional data analysis is a growing subfield with applications in various areas, including genetics and neuroscience. As a result, removal of uninformative variables has become an essential step. Traditional uninformative variable removal methods, such as those used in multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA), are limited to finite-dimensional data. This research generalizes MSSA to finite-dimensional and functional domains, integrating the Smith and Dalal (2011) score transformation. The proposed multivariate functional singular spectrum examiner (MFSSEx) model is evaluated through extensive simulations, comparing its performance to the standard MFSS and the MFSSEx with the Smith and Dalal (2011) transformation included. The results show that the MFSSEx with the score transformation included outperforms the other models. To demonstrate the applicability of this approach, researchers used it to analyze DNA methylation data from the Cancer Genome Atlas.

Consider a one-dimensional random walk $(S_n)_{n \geq 0}$ with increments of mean zero and unit variance. Given positive constants $v$ and $\lambda$, this paper investigates the probability that the walk remains within the range $[-v, v]$ for its first $ \lambda$ steps. Notably, the absence of lower moment assumptions on the distribution allows the probability to be estimated as $\frac{c(\lambda)}{v}$, where the sum of $\frac{1}{{c(k)}}$ converges, marking an improvement over the result established by Lawler and Vickers (2019).

The small-scale IShTAR experiment is designed to investigate the fundamental aspects of helicon plasmas and improve radio frequency plasma processing technologies. In its current configuration, the facility is operating with plasma sources at 20 to 30 centimeters in length, utilizing R-wave ICRP helicon modes. Theoretical models suggest that axial plasma current can be generated through the application of L-wave helicon modes in an external magnetic field, potentially leading to novel plasma-based physics effects. The initial step towards developing R-wave helicon sources involves comprehending the R-wave mode structure, characteristics, and comparing them to previously established P-wave models. The IShTAR helicon plasma source's source plate has been modified to measure the distribution of neutral atoms, electrons, and ions produced by R-wave helicon mode plasmas. The results of this study show that R-wave helicon mode plasmas generate localized concentrations of neutral atoms and ions near the source plate, with minimal loss of electrons to the source plate due to their high mass. The current model of the source is capable of accurately predicting neutral atom and ion loss to the source plate, with only the distribution of electrons near the source plate showing some discrepancy. The current source is limited by the size of the source plate, which results in the absorption of a significant amount of R-wave helicon mode energy, leading to high plasma densities that may not be suitable for many applications in small-scale plasma devices.

The microscopic examination of tissue samples is a commonplace method for cancer diagnosis, yet it requires skilled pathologists to locate and analyze individual cells, a time-consuming task. To streamline this process, researchers have been developing and refining techniques to automatically identify cell nuclei in digital images of tissue samples. Although some progress has been made, achieving high-precision results remains challenging. In this study, we present an improved two-step approach to automatically locate cell nuclei in images of tissue samples. In the first stage, a network is trained to pinpoint the boundaries of individual nuclei, and in the second stage, probabilities are assigned to each pixel indicating the likelihood of it belonging to a nucleus. This method was tested on the standard pathology dataset, showing significant improvements in accuracy compared to a single-stage approach.

We demonstrate the local converse theorem for all special orthogonal and symplectic matrices of odd dimension in all cases where the characteristic of the field is not two, thereby addressing a notable gap in the comprehensive classification of central simple algebras based on their local and global properties.

We provide a basic explanation of how Graph Convolutional Neural Networks function, demonstrating the equivalence between traditional GCN operations and matched filtering. This equivalence enables an efficient implementation of traditional GCN layers using Index-Sparse Technology, resulting in order-of-magnitude speedup. Our research also reveals the limitations of traditional GCN equivalence to certain advanced graph neural network variants. We examined the effectiveness of using matched filtering for cutting-edge applications, comparing its performance against standard approaches and optimal Index-Sparse technology. Our contributions include explicit proofs of the relationship between traditional and advanced graph neural networks, offering opportunities for optimization.

We expand our previous work (arXiv:2008.01661, arXiv:2010.05033) to incorporate a Chern-Simons term in the action of a (2+1)-dimensional gravity model coupled to a scalar field, eliminating the necessity for the scalar field to be dilaton-like. With this modified theory, we successfully describe rotating black holes with hair and point out that the charge and angular momentum must be located near the horizon to avoid repelling the matter field. Furthermore, we show that the horizonless soliton solutions in this model have no matching in the original (without scalar field) Chern-Simons theory, implying that the theory without a scalar field cannot consistently be viewed as a (quantum) gauge theory of gravity.

Researchers have developed a precise method to measure lateral tissue deformation using elastography, overcoming limitations in existing tracking algorithms that suffer from inaccurate aperture synthesis due to delayed signal processing. By proposing a novel virtual origin concept and synthesizing a virtual transducer origin, the algorithm circumvents estimation errors, requiring only a single frame acquisition in real-time applications. Initial assessments using simulated and actual data demonstrate improved deformation measurement accuracy, with root-mean-square errors significantly reduced compared to conventional algorithms, particularly in deep-tissue scenarios. This elastography algorithm's performance outperforms current standards, enabling precise medical diagnosis and treatment planning.

Traditional method instructions, like algorithms and procedures, aim to establish a connection between inputs and valuable outputs. These approaches were examined through the lens of simple artificial intelligence, by creating a new framework called "Rational Pseudocode." This framework divides instructional information into three key aspects: demonstrating the current state, explaining the purpose of an action, and describing the procedure to perform that action. We focused on the second aspect, purpose, which can be understood by analyzing demonstrations using formal methods, particularly in the form of trace explanations. This explanation style uses structured reasoning, similar to logical deductions, to connect each step of a demonstrated process to its underlying motivation. Our research shows that trace explanations extracted from real-world demonstrations can be directly applied as executable instructions, thereby establishing a direct link between guidelines and actions. Building on this concept, our study introduces two primary explanations for individual demonstration steps: background explanations, which rely on domain knowledge, and procedural explanations, which are derived from the extracted rules.

Gaussian smoothing creates a bridge between discrete and continuous settings in randomized algorithms, enabling the application of efficient data structures for balanced binary search trees. In a pursuit of a better balance, we aim to replicate the performance of the optimal static structure by Aragon and Seidel (1997) in a dynamic setting. This structure supports the fundamental operations of searching, deleting, and updating, with the cost of the latter two operations minimized to logarithmic factors in the number of elements. We achieve this with an almost linear sum of preprocessing and update costs. Moreover, the $k$-means clustering problem in terms of dimensionality, known for its difficulty, is addressed with a set of approximate factors in its dynamic version. We present an algorithm that supports fundamental operations with corresponding logarithmic dimensions, known data structures in both dimensions facilitate this balance.

To analyze the dynamics of local and regional pursuit-evasion competitions, a probabilistic approach was adopted. These competitions, at their core, reflect fundamental aspects of real-world phenomena, be it the spread of a virus within a community or the damage mitigation following an earthquake. A key aspect of our study involves developing a stochastic framework, with mathematical models incorporating various elements such as an earthquake's intensity, the damage it causes, and the pace of rescue operations. These models are highlighted through distinct examples, supported by relevant literature.

A study of standard model processes involving the emission of one vector boson and two quarks, also known as $qg\gamma/Z$ physics, serves as an efficient framework for assessing physics involving vector boson estimation at future high-energy muon colliders without $s$-channel quark antiguark scattering processes involving one vector boson, such as $\mu^+\mu^+\to q\bar{q}Z$ and $\mu^+\mu^-\to q\bar{q}\gamma/Z$. This study delves into this framework's nuances, including NLO QCD corrections and final-state hadronization, with the aid of programs like MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, Py8, and PYTHIA8. Accuracy of cross-section calculations is verified, with results closely mirroring those of prior studies, across a wide range of colliding quark flavors and for various $Z\to \ell^+\ell^-$ and $\gamma+j$ final states, across various colliding scenarios at energy levels of 3, 8, and 14 Tels, with luminosities of 1, 5, and 50 $\times 10^{34}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. This study also explores promising $s$-channel processes involving one vector boson, including VBF $Z$-boson mediated same-sign lepton pair production, and even low mass qu

Combining multiple tasks in machine learning models can lead to one task negatively influencing another during training, particularly when using a unified model for all tasks. Such negative side effects are magnified in the context of distributed training with multiple workers. This research investigates a unique setup for model-based reinforcement learning, where several workers collaborate by sharing memory, computation, and policy but operate on distinct parts of the environment. This approach offers notable advantages over a single environment setup. However, to our knowledge, it is novel for multi-task learning. This multi-task learning challenge requires agents to learn diverse states, actions, and rewards under a unified model. Although current methods are successful, we believe there's room for more efficiency and scalability. Current workers collaborating on distinct environments to share memory, computation, and policy and leverage their individual knowledge to solve complex problems successfully and efficiently. Current approaches successful but membrane-based solutions limit scalability by introducing significant communication costs. Current agents' solutions successful but limited by the need for a central controller to coordinate tasks. This leads us to propose a new, more efficient and scalable setup for model-based multi-task reinforcement learning where several workers collaborate by operating on distinct parts of the environment, sharing memory, computation, and policy but with a unique design that modules each task separately to prevent negative interference between tasks. We demonstrate the success of this design by solving the current multi-task learning setup and showing that it leads to better performance and scalability over current approaches. Our results show that our design leads to significant improvements in performance

This article historical narrative centers on four individuals: Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser. It details how they collaborated and competed within the Department of Logic at Princeton University during the 1940s and 50s.

This research extends the "three spheres theorem" from solution theory to four spheres, specifically for functions in a certain class that satisfy a particular differential equation. This equation involves the Dirac operator in Clifford analysis and these four spheres are related to three radii and two distances between their centers. The current proof technique is algebraic and it allows us to extract explicit formulas.

We propose to employ conditional generative adversarial networks to resolve inverse problems, specifically aiming to generate samples that adhere to prior constraints and align with observed data. To achieve this, we develop a constrained model capable of producing diverse, high-quality samples in accordance with the Bayesian framework. To further enhance its effectiveness, we introduce a variant of this GAN model that ensures recovered samples remain within the feasible set. Our approach is evaluated through application to tomographic reconstruction, demonstrating improved results compared to traditional methods, particularly in scenarios involving sparse data.

This study proves that in a fractional order dynamical system, specified by the parameter $ \alpha $ between 0 and 1, there is no set of conditions that guarantees the preservation of a quadratic invariant surface across three-dimensional space. Specifically, it demonstrates that, for any particular setup involving polynomial dynamics and algebraic surfaces, the measures required to maintain the invariant nature of those surfaces become increasingly complex as the parameter $ \alpha $ approaches 0 and infinity, with no finite or transcendental solution existing that would apply universally across all possible configurations.

This study delves into the interstellar medium (ISM) that scintillates the Scylla I (PSR B1133+16) pulsar signal using six years of scintillation observations from the VLA between 2014 and 2019. A total of 344,440 time-series scintillograms were analyzed to map the three-dimensional distribution of the interstellar medium around the galaxy's center. By examining the times it takes for scintillating waves to arrive, we extracted information about the pulsar's scintillation pattern. A computer algorithm helped interpret these data in order to find characteristics of the pulsar and the interstellar medium. Specifically, we determined the thickness and electron density of the region around the pulsar, as well as the density of the far-field and near-field environments. A comparison of our findings with other studies using different methods revealed that radio scintillation is an effective tool for investigating the ISM, particularly the regions near bright pulsars. Moreover, we discovered that the VLA could successfully map the interstellar medium even with limited observations of a single pulsar over several years at the 1.6 GHz frequency.

This paper introduces a novel approach called QP-WaveNet, a variant of WaveNet, to generate speech based on mel-spectrograms using only small amounts of training data. To achieve this, QP-WaveNet builds upon the WaveNet framework, which utilizes dilated convolution neural networks for predicting audio samples, and is capable of producing high-quality speech without the need for predicting entire spectra at once. Instead, it generates speech sample by sample from the waveform. QP-WaveNet's innovation lies in employing a patch-based training method, similar to SPNet, and a dilated convolution module designed to capture the fundamental frequency (F0) in the frequency domain for the purpose of speech generation. Experimental results show that the model produces significant improvements in terms of the Mean Opinion Score (MOS) and the Mean Square Error (MSE) when compared to the original WaveNet approach.

The theory of shadows constitutes an exhaustive 2-isomorphism class of extensions for a specific 2-truncated 2-category, addressing a particular aspect of homotopy theory.  This work establishes an established equivalence between shadows and bicategorical tracks, further deriving two additional equivalences – one between tracks and pseudo tracks, and another, novel equivalence between tracks and bimodules, the latter being the most locally relevant concept.  These derivations explain the origin of naming "shelves" and "modules" in the context of bimodules.

We examined our difficulties in accurately and consistently locating sound sources in a stereo listening setup, conducting this study under both echo-free and echo-filled conditions. To measure accurately, participants were asked to indicate the exact position of a sound source using a mouse, rather than a comparative method often employed in previous studies. Our findings showed that in an anechoic environment, listeners could effectively utilize intensity differences between speakers to sound source localization, a capability that was significantly hindered in the reverberant condition. Furthermore, we discovered that listeners struggled to utilize phase differences between speakers to locate sound sources, a capability not observed in the anechoic condition. To better understand these difficulties, we utilized a simplified version of a sound localization model, which successfully captured the key features of our participants' experiences. Our study contributes essential data on low-level sound source localization challenges that are often overlooked in current research.

Recent advancements in using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been hindered by the challenges of scaling to large datasets and avoiding the oversimplification of data through Euclidean assumptions. A proposed solution, Linear Graph Neural Networks (LGNNs), overcomes these limitations by providing linear scaling and leveraging least-squares solutions for solving message-passing equations. This solution ensures robustness against common GNN issues such as message accumulation and broadcasting. The efficacy of LGNNs has been demonstrated with improved performance on transductive graph classification and satisfactory results in semi-supervised node classification and graph classification tasks.

This research focuses on solving a reverse problem for a structural acoustic system. We consider a stochastic differential equation that describes the movement of a structure interacting with an enclosed acoustic space. The structure's movement is modeled as a smooth transformation of space, with additional equations describing the structure's movement and the air's compression within the enclosure. We establish an implicit relationship between two probabilistic measures that are related to these equations, and this connection is approximated using a new implicit numerical scheme. This scheme is proven to provide precise solutions with convergence rates, enabling us to address the reverse problem and related options in structural acoustic engagements.

We developed a novel efficient delay discounting model, which is both robust and resistant to criticism, by applying the principles of the Tsallis formalism. This model, belonging to the class of exponential family distributions, demonstrates resistance to a broad class of alternative models through the incorporation of a single, non-trivial parameter. Our analysis involved three key areas: an examination of the efficient q-logistic delay discounting function, an exploration of impulse decisions through a variant of the intertemporal choice problem, and an investigation into consumption decisions utilizing a modified version of the golden rule problem.

Recently, a new gravity theory called substantial gravity (SG) was introduced, which is second-order in a metric tensor and ensures the energy of gravitational fields is always positive, especially in a flat spacetime framework. SG demonstrates its equivalence to Anti-de Sitter (AdS) gravity when the dimensionless parameter in SG is set to its -1 counterpart in AdS gravity. This comparison between the two theories supports the idea that SG is not merely an unnecessary extension of AdS gravity. SG's action framework allows for the application of harmonic gauge, which can be made simpler by choosing an appropriate gauge transformation. This approach may provide a straightforward path to quantizing SG by perturbation around Minkowski space, in contrast to the usual quadratic Fock-Tonantz scalar gauge used in AdS gravity.

This research examines the Wojo-Wigner symbol of the canonical conditions required for thermal and mechanical equilibrium. 
By reviewing these requirements, we investigate how a system achieves equilibrium with its surroundings through thermal contact or by undergoing expansion in a fixed container. 
Our analysis of these canonical situations is conducted from a quantum thermodynamic standpoint. 
Our study is further extended to examine analogous conditions for radiative equilibrium. 
When in a cavity filled with radiation, the canonical conditions lead to a Planckian distribution of a quantum field. 
When examining a system undergoing expansion in a fixed container, the canonical conditions result in a non-equilibrium steady-state that remains constant given unvarying temperature and volume conditions. 
When examining Weyl-Wigner symbols of the canonical conditions for a harmonic oscillator, we observe that the canonical thermal and mechanical equilibrium conditions for a constant volume lead to the Bessel differential equation in two dimensions.

The notion of negative temperature, first introduced by Sir William Thomson in 1849, holds significant theoretical importance but limited practical applications. According to William Thomson's definition, negative temperature indicates a situation where adding heat to a substance causes it to cool down, contradicting our everyday experiences. The purpose of this commentary is to present a more positive perspective on absolute temperature, regardless of whether it is above or below zero, by reinterpreting the meaning of negative temperatures through the lens of statistical mechanics. This new understanding allows us to recognize the practical utility of negative temperatures in determining the direction of spontaneous heat flow and assessing the efficiency of heat engines, as well as clarifying the meaningfulness of the Kelvin scale's origin and direction.

By extending the Standard Model with an additional scalar doublet and a triplet in both the dark sector and the electroweak sector, the minimal scoto-seesaw model is established. This model effectively accounts for the neutrino mass and scale through the dark sector's interaction with the electroweak sector. By analyzing the potential of the model, we determine the conditions under which the dark sector remains stable, the electroweak scale remains secure, and neutrinos acquire mass through radiative correction. By explicitly calculating the corrections to the light neutrino mass matrix and incorporating the dark sector's parameters, we can derive constraints on the weak scale. This calculation reveals that a specific combination of the dark sector parameters must lie within a limited range to satisfy theoretical requirements. However, such a condition is inconsistent with the need for WIMP dark matter to thermally produce the observed abundance. This discrepancy suggests that the minimal scoto-seesaw framework with a dark sector containing a complex scalar and a fermion is insufficient to explain neutrino mass and scale while also accounting for WIMP dark matter.

In this paper, we investigate the characteristics of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital angular brackets in transition metal compounds, noting that conventional wisdom suggests blending these two types of orbitals is impossible due to symmetry. We begin by examining the symmetries present in octahedral, tetrahedral, and square planar geometries. Next, we analyze tetragonal distortions of tetrahedral geometries found in spinel compounds and explain why the blending of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitars occurs in tetrahedral and tetragonal geometries. Finally, we explore the effects of blending $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals on the physical properties of 4d and 5d transition metal spinel compounds.

This study focuses on a new quantum topological invariant, known as relative quantum $Q$-homology, which applies to a pair consisting of a three-dimensional variety and divisors with specific properties. Notably, we discover that this invariant remains consistent, even when the pair undergoes certain mathematical transformations called birational alterations, provided certain conditions are met. As a result of this invariance, we are able to develop a quantum version of Birkhoff factorization, leading to intrinsic invariant theories for a class of special divisor-rich varieties called GLasserman-Tschinkel pairs.

Deepest visual task advancements have profoundly impacted medical imaging analysis, yet most studies focus on analyzing existing data rather than altering it. Nonetheless, modifying existing visuals to address specific concerns or address deficiencies is equally important in the medical imaging context. This paper introduces two novel applications of visual transformation in medicine: explaining current flaws and predicting future problems. We present two new disciplines of illustration transformation called "illness-aware inverse visualization" and "illness-aware future prediction". Based on these concepts, this study presents two novel frameworks that integrate existing analysis tasks with reverse transformation models to achieve "illness-aware inverse visualization" and "illness-aware future prediction". We apply these concepts to create two demonstration scenarios for analyzing existing data, involving the modification of ethnic identity in face analysis and age in face analysis, and promising directions for future research on studying chest X-rays are explored.

ViDaExpert is an MATLAB-based application for multidimensional vector visualization and thorough examination. This tool enables users to visualize relationships between various dimensions, perform interactive scalar operations, and explore subsets of the data. Additionally, ViDaExpert includes a subset visualization feature that facilitates the subset's examination through scalar operations, histogram analysis, and pairwise plotting. With a focus on usability, ViDaExamert allows for a range of actions including zooming, panning, rescaling, and color adjustment to aid in data understanding.
